title: My week as a tax radical
gist: Oxford political scientist Ben Ansell recounts the tabloid backlash to his IPPR proposal that working over-65s earning above £50,000 pay an extra 2 per cent national insurance, and argues the UK tax burden is shifting unfairly onto the working-age young. He predicts the government will avoid major tax rises before the budget, while urging broad, boring tax increases instead.

insights.claim: Ansell's IPPR paper proposed that working Britons over 65 earning above £50,000 pay an extra 2 per cent national insurance, meaning an employed pensioner on £60,000 would pay about £200 more a year.
insights.so_what: Shows how small the proposed pensioner tax change was relative to the political backlash it triggered.
insights.quote: An employed pensioner making £60,000 a year would thus pay an extra £200 annually
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: A millennial doctor on £105,000 with post-2012 student loans and children can face an effective marginal tax rate of 71 pence in the pound due to loan repayments and lost child benefit, tax-free childcare and personal allowance.
insights.so_what: Extreme marginal rates on high-earning young workers can depress labour supply and productivity in the UK.
insights.quote: does it really make sense for them to pay tax at a rate of 71 pence in the pound?
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: Graduates who attended university after 2012 effectively face an extra 9 per cent surcharge on income tax to repay fees.
insights.so_what: Higher effective taxation of younger cohorts weighs on their disposable income and consumption.
insights.quote: Younger Brits who went to university after 2012 face an extra 9 per cent surcharge on their income tax to pay back fees.
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: UK fiscal spending will be some 10 per cent of national income higher by 2075 because of the demands of an ageing population.
insights.so_what: Long-run fiscal pressure from ageing is a structural risk for gilts and future tax levels.
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: UK parties are competing to protect pensioners, with Andy Burnham guaranteeing the triple lock until 2030 and moves to lift the personal allowance so state pension income is untaxed.
insights.so_what: Locks in rising pension spending, constraining fiscal room and raising borrowing needs.
insights.locator: What is our national political response
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats both want to raise the personal allowance to £15,000, funded respectively by policies on immigration and closer relations with Europe.
insights.so_what: Cross-party unfunded tax-cut pledges heighten UK fiscal credibility risk.
insights.quote: Both want to raise the personal allowance to £15,000
insights.locator: What is our national political response
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: Ansell argues that, contrary to political rhetoric, taxes are being piled ever higher on the working-age population while pensioners are shielded.
insights.so_what: Intergenerational fiscal tension is a growing driver of UK political realignment.
insights.quote: taxes are piled ever-higher on the backs of the working-age population
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: Ansell predicts the government is unlikely to risk major tax rises in the upcoming budget, while Chancellor John Healey must fund higher defence spending, the triple lock and climbing interest payments.
insights.so_what: Avoiding tax rises amid rising commitments raises UK deficit and gilt supply risk.
insights.quote: As budget day approaches, it seems unlikely the government will risk political death by taxation.
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: Budgets under Rachel Reeves had already shifted many tax rises needed to satisfy the Office for Budget Responsibility to the eve of the next general election.
insights.so_what: Back-loaded tax rises create pre-election fiscal cliff and credibility risk.
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: Ansell argues big broad-based tax rises can succeed politically, citing George Osborne's 2010 VAT and capital gains tax increases, which voters remember less than the later pasty tax.
insights.so_what: Suggests VAT-style broad taxes are the most politically viable revenue levers for UK governments.
insights.quote: just go big and raise taxes that are too boring and broad-based to create good tabloid headlines
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell

insights.claim: The IPPR report also proposed merging council tax and stamp duty into a proportional property tax and taxing artificial intelligence tokens.
insights.so_what: AI-token taxation and property-tax reform are live ideas in UK centre-left policy circles.
insights.locator: Now, there was lots of other stuff
insights.speaker: Ben Ansell
